title: Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development
content:
## 2.1 Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development

**Instrument logic and target outcome.** FIELDWISE is structured as a European Postdoctoral Fellowship hosted by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) in Hungary, comprising a 24-month research and training period at ELTE followed by a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR (M25–M30), for a total action of 30 months. The whole design of the training and mobility programme is oriented to the call's central postdoctoral outcome — an increased set of research and transferable skills leading to improved employability and career prospects within academia and beyond (Expected Outcome EO-01) — and to the corresponding societal impact of improved researcher employability and career mobility within and beyond academia (EI-01). The measures below are credible precisely because they are not generic: they are engineered around the specific competence gap between the researcher's confirmed starting profile and the profile FIELDWISE builds, and each measure is tied to a named mechanism, a responsible party and, where the call requires it, a verifiable deliverable.

**The Career Development Plan as the governing instrument.** The career and skills programme is consolidated in a single governing instrument, the Career Development Plan (deliverable D1.3), established jointly by the supervisors and the researcher and submitted as an early deliverable due in month 3 (M3). It is signed by both the supervisor and the co-supervisor together with the fellow, satisfying the call requirement that the plan be established jointly by supervisor(s) and researcher (scope requirement SR-05). The plan is not a static document: it is agreed by M3 and formally reviewed at all five Project Steering Group points (M6, M12, M16, M20 and M27), the last of which falls inside the placement window, when non-academic career development is most in play. Its adoption and review are tracked as a measurable performance indicator (KPI K11: 'Career Development Plan agreed by M3 and reviewed at all five steering points'), so the plan is auditable rather than aspirational. The plan spans six components — research objectives (O1–O6); training and career needs; transferable skills; teaching; publications planning; and open-science engagement — which together turn the abstract commitment to 'career development' into a scheduled, reviewed programme owned by named people.

**Specific skills-development measures.** The proposal specifies three interlocking mechanisms for skills acquisition. First, structured discipline-specific training: ELTE transfers eleven confirmed competences to the fellow — geoinformatics; EO time-series analysis; optical/SAR integration; hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer; spatio-temporal modelling; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; uncertainty quantification; transfer learning/domain adaptation; reproducible geospatial computation; research software/web deployment; and IP and research exploitation — delivered as supervised practice embedded in the work packages plus named ELTE short-course provision. Consolidated, the fellowship delivers advanced competence in Bayesian/probabilistic modelling, uncertainty quantification, spatio-temporal validation, sensor-domain transfer, cross-country adaptation, operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and IP/exploitation. This is exactly the competence gap the researcher currently carries (Bayesian modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor transfer, uncertainty, domain adaptation and decision evaluation), so the training is calibrated to a real, stated deficit rather than to a template. Second, seven transferable-skill strands are embedded in the plan — research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication — directly answering the call's requirement that training integrate key transferable skills and competences, including digital skills such as generative AI, and foster Open Science culture, knowledge valorisation and research integrity (SR-04). Third, an intensive and progressive supervision regime supports both: a weekly one-to-one meeting with the supervisor, Prof. András Jung; a weekly technical session with the co-supervisor, Dr. Roland Hollós, who provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing across the modelling-intensive work packages WP3 (Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction) and WP4 (Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability); a monthly written progress record held by the fellow; and a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors. The skills transfer is genuinely bidirectional — the fellow brings plant physiology, horticultural crop science, water-stress experimentation and hyperspectral field measurement into a geoinformatics faculty, while the faculty supplies the geospatial and data-science competence — so the fellowship enriches the host as well as the researcher and demonstrates a two-way knowledge flow rather than one-directional apprenticeship.

**Employability outside academia: the non-academic placement.** Employability beyond academia is addressed structurally, not rhetorically, through the six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR, taken at the end of the action under the optional up-to-six-months provision (SR-06) and made an integral, justified part of the proposal. The placement supplies the inter-sectoral half of the intended career progression that the academic host cannot provide: operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and direct exposure to commercial agricultural-software requirements. Its six-month work content is concrete and confirmed — operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production farm-management-information-system environment; the nine-dimension operational assessment producing the deliverable AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4); the FMIS integration roadmap written from inside the implementing company, producing the deliverable FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5); and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers. What the placement gives that ELTE cannot is a production FMIS environment, a commercial engineering practice and direct contact with paying growers — none of which is available in a research infrastructure. This is the segment of the profile that makes the researcher employable in precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and FMIS companies as well as in academia, and it is designed so that the placement serves the fellow's training rather than the host company's engineering. The placement is hosted at AgroVIR in Budaörs, Hungary, an EU Member State, and is subject to evaluation as the Guide for Applicants requires.

**Teaching and dissemination as career assets.** Two further measures broaden the professional profile. The fellow will co-design and deliver a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, and will co-supervise the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work — measures framed not as competences to be acquired but as an existing five-year university-teaching strength transferred into a new discipline, a new institution and a new language of instruction, and stepped up toward doctoral supervision, thereby feeding research results back into higher education (EI-06). Scientific dissemination is planned around four principal outputs (P1–P4) with at least two peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship, alongside public engagement beyond scientific peers, strengthening the networking and communication capacity that underpins an independent research career.

**Expected contribution to the future career of the researcher.** Taken together, these measures target a specific, stated progression: from Plant Physiologist/Agronomist, through EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist, to an Independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence. The fellowship builds a distinctive scientific profile that combines biological understanding with scalable geospatial prediction and operational agricultural decision support — a combination that is scarce and that the researcher's current profile in agronomy, plant protection and plant physiology, augmented by developing EO, GIS and agricultural-data-science expertise, does not yet reach. By taking a scientific concept through the full chain of experimental evidence, validated model, cross-country testing, commercial-field testing and web MVP, the researcher acquires an end-to-end, research-to-operation competence set that is directly relevant to European research institutes, universities, EU agricultural and environmental research, EO organisations, precision-agriculture companies, irrigation technology and FMIS providers. The credibility of the employability claim rests on this breadth: the academic period equips the fellow for an independent academic trajectory (advanced modelling, uncertainty, transferability, IP/exploitation, teaching and publications), while the inter-sectoral placement demonstrably widens the addressable market to the non-academic sector. The Career Development Plan, with its M3 baseline and five scheduled reviews, is the mechanism that keeps this trajectory on track and adaptable, so that the skills development translates into concrete, evidenced career advancement rather than an untracked intention.
